title: Havdalah and the Extra Soul
carry: shabbat brings an extra soul; spices see it off
tomorrow: Noa's college calendar collides with the holidays. now what?

cards: Coffee smells like morning. Sunscreen smells like summer. In Jewish homes on Saturday night, a little box of cloves or cinnamon, passed from hand to hand, smells like Shabbat leaving.
That's havdalah, the goodbye. Noa is packing the small spice box Saba gave her, and her dorm has a rule: no open flames.

teach.b: The Torah gives the Shabbat command twice, in two words. Exodus: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy." Deuteronomy: "Observe the sabbath day, to keep it holy."

The Talmud teaches that God said both in a single utterance, something no human mouth can do, and the Friday-night song Lecha Dodi sings that line. So Shabbat has two sides: remembering it, and keeping it.
And it arrives through the senses. Candlelight on Friday. Wine for kiddush.
Challah under a cloth. At the end, the spices.

teach.h: CANDLES TO SPICES: AN EXTRA SOUL.
teach.b: The Talmud says a person is given an extra soul on Shabbat, and that it's taken back when Shabbat ends; tradition connects the spices with that moment, a breath of sweetness for the week ahead.
Jewish communities differ on what keeping Shabbat requires, from every law of the day to a meal and candles and phones away.
The Shabbat that became yours is the one you actually remember and keep.
Something to tell a friend tonight: the Torah says remember in one place and observe in another, and the Talmud says God spoke them as one.

how: Shabbat begins Friday evening with candles, kiddush over wine and challah, and ends Saturday night with havdalah, a short ceremony with wine, a braided candle and fragrant spices; observance ranges from keeping all of its laws to keeping parts of it.

games.q: your partner didn't grow up with Shabbat. on Friday he asks, 'so what are we actually supposed to do?' what fits today?
o: start with what you both can keep: a meal, candles, phones away, spices Saturday night.
do every law of the day perfectly from the start, or wait until you can.
it's just a day off, so anything goes as long as you rest a bit.
games.why: Shabbat is remember and observe, and it arrives through the senses. communities differ on what keeping it requires; the one you actually keep becomes yours.

practice: Find something fragrant nearby: a clove, cinnamon, coffee beans, an orange peel. Hold it close and breathe it in slowly, a few times, the way people do at havdalah. Let the smell mark one week ending and the next one starting.
